name: composite-entity
intent: Represent a cluster of related, dependent objects through one coarse-grained entity that owns them and persists and synchronises the whole graph as a single unit of work, so clients never reference, sequence, or save the parts themselves. Coined for coarse-grained EJB business objects; its modern form is the aggregate root with cascading or owned mappings.
problem: A business concept clients treat as one thing (an order with its lines, a customer with addresses) is really a cluster of dependent objects, and persisting each part separately forces callers to know the parts, save them in the right order in the right transaction, delete the ones that left the relationship, and absorb a leaking physical schema. The catalog trigger: a cluster of related objects must persist and synchronise as one unit.
context: Relational or document stores where a coarse-grained business object is composed of finer-grained dependent objects whose lifecycle is bound to it. Applies when clients - especially remote ones - should exchange one coarse-grained structure instead of the parts, when the persist/synchronise boundary must coincide with one transaction, and when each dependent can still own its own mapping. Modern form: an aggregate root mapped with cascading associations or with components stored in the root's own row.
benefits: Clients see one coarse-grained object and one save operation instead of a graph they must sequence themselves; the physical schema stays hidden behind the composite.
Consistency: the cluster commits or rolls back as one unit, so callers cannot leave a half-saved or orphaned graph behind.
Fewer round trips and no chatty per-dependent access - the classic motivation for coarse-grained entity beans, and still the reason to expose one structure over a remote boundary.
Dependent objects keep their own persistence knowledge, so the same dependent type can be reused in several composites and its mapping can change independently of the root.
Schema evolution is localised: table or column changes land in the dependent mappers, not in every client.
Composite transfer objects come almost free: the root already knows how to gather its dependents into the coarse-grained shape clients receive.
tradeoffs: The unit is loaded and saved whole, so partial reads and partial writes are not expressible without escaping the composite; narrow use cases over-fetch an entire cluster.
Long-lived composites drift towards god aggregates: unrelated concerns accrete into one root, widening the transaction and coupling teams that should not share a commit.
Write amplification and lost updates: a cascading save rewrites every dependent it holds, so concurrent edits by another transaction are overwritten wholesale.
Stale in-memory graphs unless the discipline holds that only the root mutates its dependents - a second write path (direct repository, bulk update) silently desynchronises the cluster.
Coarser concurrency granularity: locking or versioning the root means unrelated edits to different dependents conflict (see Coarse-Grained Lock).

Implicit cascade writes are a data-loss and security hazard: frameworks document that cascade/owning relationships persist whatever object happens to be attached, and that removal is only driven by loaded relations.

participants.responsibility: Coarse-grained object representing the cluster; the only entry point clients and mappers use, and the owner of the dependents' lifecycle.
The persistable representative of the composite - classic: the entity bean holding the dependents; modern: the aggregate root row that carries the cluster identity and is loaded/saved as the unit.
Fine-grained part with its own data and mapping; it is created, changed and removed through the composite and has no independent access path from clients.
Knows how one dependent (or the root) is read and written - SQL, table, columns - so the cluster can be persisted without the composite embedding store details.
Tracks the whole cluster's changes during a transaction and flushes them once; in the classic form this was the EJB container's transaction, today it is the ORM session or persistence context.
Works with the coarse-grained interface (often a composite transfer object) and never with the individual dependent objects.

use_cases: Order with line items, shipment addresses and payment allocations that must be written and deleted as one business unit.
Customer or account aggregate holding addresses, contact methods and preferences that are edited in one form and saved once.
Document-style clusters (invoice with revisions, article with embedded sections) where the parts only exist inside the root.
Legacy-style coarse-grained entity beans that wrap fine-grained POJOs so that clients exchange one composite transfer object instead of many fine-grained ones.
Mobile or remote clients that must send one coarse-grained payload per edit instead of a sequence of dependent calls.
Batch imports where a cluster is validated and written transactionally, so a partially imported entity never exists.

DDD Bounded Contexts where one aggregate encapsulates a complete business invariant enforced across multiple related entities — e.g., a Rental aggregate containing a rental agreement, reserved vehicle, and driver assignment that must all be created or fail together.
CQRS write models where the aggregate is the sole write target and all state changes flow through the root's command methods, ensuring every mutation is a coherent cluster-level operation.

Event sourcing snapshots where the aggregate root serialises its entire graph so that snapshot restore reconstructs the full composite in one operation rather than re-playing individual dependent events.
Legacy system facades that wrap a network of fine-grained remote beans behind a single coarse-grained composite interface, collapsing many remote calls into one round-trip for external clients.

SQLAlchemy parent-child clusters mapped with cascade='all, delete-orphan' on relationship(): disassociating a child deletes the row, so the Session flushes the cluster as one unit without per-child Session.delete() calls.
EF Core owned types: dependent types stored in the owner's table (or as owned navigations) share the aggregate root's identity and save with a single context.SaveChanges().
Mongoose subdocument arrays: embedded parts are saved, validated and removed through the top-level document, so the cluster's lifecycle is bound to the root document's save.
avoid_when: The parts have their own identity and lifecycle and are referenced from outside the cluster - use Dependent Mapping only if the child really has no independent persistence, otherwise plain Foreign Key Mapping with independent aggregates.
Clients legitimately need narrow, high-volume access to single dependents: a full coarser aggregate adds over-fetch - use Data Mapper with Lazy Load on the parts instead.
The store is a document database and the cluster is naturally one document (Mongoose-style subdocuments): embedding is then a store decision, not an entity-pattern decision.
The transaction is short and already coordinated by a repository plus Unit of Work, and no coarse-grained exchange object is needed - the composite adds an indirection layer for nothing.
The cluster is unbounded (audit trails, event logs, large collections): loading it as one entity is a scalability bug - keep those parts as separate aggregates or Serialized LOB.
You only need to hide the schema, not to group objects: a Data Access Object or Repository achieves that with less coupling.
anti_patterns: Fat aggregate root: unrelated objects folded into one composite so that every edit touches the same transaction, turning one coarse-grained entity into a god object.
Composite without lifecycle rules - dependents added and removed freely while nothing deletes the orphans, so the store accumulates rows the domain has forgotten.
Rebuilding the pattern by hand on top of a framework that already implements it (JPA cascades, EF Core owned types, Mongoose subdocuments) and thereby reintroducing per-dependent save calls.
Using Composite Entity as an excuse for cascade-everything mappings that persist any object that happens to be attached to the relation.
Coarse-grained entity as a distributed facade: making the composite remote again (fine-grained remote calls, one entity bean per table) recreates the network overhead the pattern removes.
design_principles: Information hiding: the physical schema and the parts' mapping stay behind the coarse-grained object.
Single responsibility per role: the root coordinates the transaction, each dependent maps itself, the unit of work flushes once.
High cohesion with a clear boundary: only objects whose lifecycle truly coincides belong to the composite (aggregate boundary).
Open/closed at the cluster level: new dependent types are added to the composite's mapping without changing its clients.
Encapsulation of invariants: the root is the only mutator, so it can enforce the consistency rules of the whole cluster.
best_practices: Draw the boundary from the lifecycle, not from the object diagram: a dependent belongs to the composite only if it cannot outlive it.
Expose coarse-grained operations on the root (addLine, removeLine, reprice) and keep dependents' setters private to the composite.
Persist the cluster inside exactly one unit of work, and make the dependent-removal rule explicit in the mapping so removal deletes the row.
Back the relationship with a database-level ON DELETE CASCADE so no partial graph can outlive a failure in the middle of a save.
Hand remote callers a composite transfer object and keep the live cluster server-side.
Keep the composite small enough to load in one transaction; split anything unbounded into its own aggregate, or map it lazily.

Version the root entity for optimistic concurrency control (@Version in JPA, rowversion in EF Core) so concurrent edits to different dependents conflict predictably rather than silently overwriting each other.
Enforce all cluster-level invariants inside the root's mutation methods; never let callers mutate a dependent field without going through the root's operation, or the invariant breaks silently.
Use lazy loading proxies or bytecode enhancement only for dependent traversal, never as an escape hatch to bypass the root's encapsulation and load dependents independently.
Fire domain events from the aggregate root only, after the Unit of Work has committed, to keep side effects decoupled from persistence boundaries.
Test the aggregate as a whole using repository-based integration tests; unit-testing individual dependent entities in isolation misses the cluster-level invariant violations that matter.
Reserve cascade="all" and orphanRemoval=true for true composition; use explicit CascadeType values otherwise — wildcards persist any object accidentally attached to the relationship.

related_patterns_notes.dependent-mapping: The composite entity's dependent objects are mapped in Dependent Mapping — the child's persistence logic is delegated to the parent's mapper rather than having an independent mapping path.
related_patterns_notes.unit-of-work: The Unit of Work is the transaction context a Composite Entity relies on: it tracks the dirty graph of the whole cluster and flushes all changes atomically in one commit.
related_patterns_notes.data-mapper: The composite entity's persistence manager is a specialised Data Mapper: it knows how to load and save the entire cluster from the physical schema without leaking store details into clients.
related_patterns_notes.aggregate: The DDD Aggregate is the strategic counterpart of the Composite Entity. Both represent a cluster persisted as one unit; Composite Entity is the persistence-tactical pattern (EAA), Aggregate is the domain-modelling战略 pattern (DDD). The aggregate root is the same concept as the composite entity's coarse-grained owner.
related_patterns_notes.composite: The Gang of Four Composite pattern shares the tree-structured client-facing interface but differs in intent: Composite is for UI/structural hierarchies, while Composite Entity is for transactional object graph ownership and persistence.
related_patterns_notes.whole-part: Whole-Part is a broader structural pattern for decomposing systems into constituent pieces; Composite Entity is a specific application of Whole-Part applied to the persistence domain with transactional commit semantics.
related_patterns_notes.coarse-grained-lock: Coarse-Grained Lock is the natural concurrency partner of Composite Entity: locking the root entity implicitly locks all its dependent objects, preventing inconsistent states where one thread reads a partially-updated graph.
related_patterns_notes.lazy-load: Lazy loading enables dependent objects to be loaded on demand inside the composite, but if used to bypass the root's encapsulation (loading dependents directly from the repository) it subverts the transactional boundary the composite was designed to protect.
